say.en: After a whole module of theory, two real chips: a small ARM core found in phones, and an Intel desktop processor. Every idea from this module shows up in them.

do.text: Case studies: Cortex-A53 and Core i7

say.en: Here are the eight stages.
The two processors, then each one's caches and address translation.
Then side by side with AMAT, why they differ, and an exam question.
Stage 1: two very different processors.

do.text: Stage 1 of 8: two processors

say.en: The ARM Cortex-A53 is everywhere: phones, the Raspberry Pi 3, embedded boards. The Core i7-6700 is a 2015 desktop chip from Intel's Skylake family.
The A53 has a short 8-stage pipeline, issuing 2 instructions per cycle, in order. The i7 is 4-wide and out of order, with a much deeper pipeline.
The A53 runs at about 1.2 to 2 gigahertz, the i7 at 3.4, boosting to 4.
And the goals are opposite. The A53 is built for low power and a small area. The i7 is built for speed on one thread.

do.text: same ideas, opposite goals: power versus speed

say.en: Stage 2: the A53's caches. The latencies here were measured on a board running at 1.5 gigahertz.

do.text: Stage 2 of 8: the Cortex-A53's caches

say.en: Two L1 caches per core, instructions and data. ARM lets the chip maker pick each size, from 8 to 64 kilobytes. A small chip saves area; a phone chip may pick 32.
The instruction cache is 2-way, the data cache 4-way. Both use 64 byte lines. A data hit takes 3 cycles.
The L2 is shared by all the cores, 128 kilobytes to 2 megabytes, and 16-way. A hit takes about 15 cycles.
There is no L3. A miss in L2 goes to memory: 15 cycles plus about 128 nanoseconds. At 1.5 gigahertz that is about 207 cycles.

do.text: A53: L1 3 cycles · L2 15 · memory ≈ 200

say.en: Look at the indexing. The instruction cache is virtually indexed, VIPT. The data cache is physically indexed, PIPT. Why?
Apply the VIPT condition from earlier: size over ways must not exceed the page size.
The A53's 32 kilobyte, 4-way data cache gives 8 kilobytes per way, more than a 4 kilobyte page. So it cannot simply index with the virtual address. It translates first.
The i7's 32 kilobyte cache uses 8 ways: exactly 4 kilobytes per way. So it can be VIPT. Remember that when we reach the i7.

do.text: more ways can make VIPT possible

say.en: Stage 3: if the A53 translates before every data access, translation must be very fast.

do.text: Stage 3 of 8: the A53's address translation

say.en: So it has a micro TLB of just 10 entries. Tiny, so it answers almost instantly.
Behind it, a main TLB of 512 entries, 4-way. A micro TLB miss that hits here costs only a couple of cycles.
If both miss, a page walk cache of 64 entries keeps the upper levels of the page table, so most walks skip straight to the last level.
And the walk itself is done in hardware, reading page table entries through the L2 cache. This is the TLB hierarchy we built in the virtual memory video, in miniature.

do.text: micro TLB 10 → main TLB 512 → walk cache → page walk

say.en: Stage 4: the Core i7-6700. Its latencies were measured at 4 gigahertz.

do.text: Stage 4 of 8: the Core i7-6700's caches

say.en: Each of the 4 cores has 32 kilobytes of instruction cache and 32 of data, both 8-way with 64 byte lines. A data hit takes 4 cycles.
Each core also has a private L2 of 256 kilobytes, 4-way, at 12 cycles.
Then an L3 of 8 megabytes, 16-way, shared by all four cores, at about 42 cycles. It is inclusive: everything in the L1s and L2s is also in L3, which makes checking other cores' data simpler.
Memory is DDR4-2133 on two channels. A miss all the way out costs about 42 cycles plus 51 nanoseconds: about 246 cycles at 4 gigahertz.

do.text: i7: L1 4 · L2 12 · L3 ≈ 42 · memory ≈ 246 cycles

say.en: Stage 5: the i7's translation.

do.text: Stage 5 of 8: the i7's TLBs and memory

say.en: Separate first-level TLBs: 128 entries for instructions, 8-way, and 64 entries for data, 4-way.
Behind them, a shared second-level TLB of 1536 entries, 12-way, that also holds entries for 2 megabyte pages. A data TLB miss that hits here costs about 9 cycles.
Virtual addresses are 48 bits, with the 4-level page table we drew earlier, walked in hardware.
Some numbers. Peak memory bandwidth: 2 channels, times 2133 million transfers, times 8 bytes. About 34.1 gigabytes per second.
TLB reach with 4 kilobyte pages: the 64-entry data TLB covers 256 kilobytes, the 1536-entry L2 TLB 6 megabytes.
With 2 megabyte pages, the L2 TLB covers 3 gigabytes. That is why databases and virtual machines ask for huge pages.

do.text: TLB reach = entries × page size

say.en: Stage 6: side by side.

do.text: Stage 6 of 8: side by side

say.en: Two cache levels against three. The A53's L1 is configurable and physically indexed; the i7's is fixed, 8-way, and virtually indexed.
The A53's last level is a small, fast L2. The i7's is a big L3, three times slower to reach, but four times larger.
Memory costs a similar number of cycles in both, about 200 to 250. But the i7's cycles are almost three times shorter.
Now AMAT. The latencies are measured, with the A53's memory rounded to 200 cycles. The miss rates are assumptions, for illustration.
A53: 3, plus 0.05 times, 15 plus 0.3 times 200. 6.75 cycles. At 1.5 gigahertz, 4.5 nanoseconds.
i7: 4, plus 0.05 times, 12 plus 0.3 times, 42 plus 0.2 times 246. About 6 cycles. At 4 gigahertz, about 1.5 nanoseconds.
Similar in cycles, three times apart in time. The extra L3 keeps the i7's AMAT low even though memory is farther away in cycles.

do.text: compare AMAT in nanoseconds, not just cycles

say.en: Stage 7: why did the designers choose so differently? Every row is a trade-off from this module.

do.text: Stage 7 of 8: why they differ

say.en: L1 size: ARM lets small chips save area. Intel fixes 32 kilobytes, the largest that still hits in 4 cycles at 4 gigahertz.
Indexing: the A53 pays for translation with a tiny micro TLB. The i7 uses 8 ways precisely so that VIPT works.
Levels: an L3 costs power and area that a phone core cannot spare. The i7 spends them to hide memory.
And out-of-order execution: when the A53 misses, its in-order pipeline waits. The i7 keeps running, with many misses in flight, the nonblocking caches of the advanced optimizations video.
Prefetching follows the same pattern: simple on the A53, several aggressive prefetchers on the i7.

do.text: every design choice is a trade-off you can now compute

say.en: Now the exam question.

do.text: Exam question

say.en: With 4 kilobyte pages: which L1 data cache can be VIPT? And the TLB reach of the A53's main TLB and the i7's L2 TLB.
The i7's peak memory bandwidth. And the A53's AMAT with L1 3 cycles, L2 15, memory 200, an L1 miss rate of 4 percent and an L2 local miss rate of 25. Pause and work it out.
a: the A53 has 32 over 4, 8 kilobytes per way, too big: no. The i7 has 32 over 8, 4 kilobytes: yes.
b: 512 times 4 kilobytes is 2 megabytes. 1536 times 4 kilobytes is 6 megabytes.
c: 2 times 2133 million times 8 bytes: about 34.1 gigabytes per second.
d: 15 plus 0.25 times 200 is 65. 3 plus 0.04 times 65: 5.6 cycles.
The usual slips: forgetting that DDR's number already counts both clock edges, and using an L2's global miss rate where the formula needs the local one.

do.text: know which rate is local and which is global

say.en: Let us walk the stages again.

do.text: Recap

say.en: The A53: small configurable caches, two levels, a physically indexed L1 data cache, and a tiny micro TLB to keep translation fast.
The i7: three levels with a shared inclusive L3, an 8-way VIPT L1, large TLBs, and out-of-order execution to overlap misses.
Compare them in nanoseconds, and read every choice as a trade-off. That completes Module 2, the memory hierarchy.
